explanations.answer: God's Tent of Meeting was there
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives, friend. Gibeon had God's Tent of Meeting, which Moses, the servant of the LORD, had made in the wilderness. So Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, wasn't just picking a nice hilltop for a field trip. He went where the Tent was, and he took the whole assembly with him.

Nice guess, but the text doesn't say a word about a burial at Gibeon. It says they went because that was the location of God's Tent of Meeting. As for David, the Bible says he was buried in the City of David (1 Kings 2:10). Hold on to the Tent of Meeting, friend, that's the reason.

explanations.answer: The ark of God was kept there
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, since the ark and the Tent feel like a package deal. But the text splits them up. Gibeon had the Tent of Meeting, and David had already brought the ark to the place he'd prepared for it in Jerusalem. Two different spots, friend, so keep a little map in your head.

Jerusalem it is. David brought the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it, because he had pitched a tent for it there. So the ark was in Jerusalem while the Tent of Meeting stood at Gibeon. Two places, friend, and you kept them straight.

Hebron is a fine town, but it's not the one in this verse. The text says David pitched a tent for the ark in Jerusalem, the place he had prepared for it. That's where the ark went after Kiriath-jearim. Hold on to Jerusalem, friend.

Bethel doesn't show up in this passage at all. The text says David brought the ark from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it, and he pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem. That's the place to hold on to. Jerusalem, friend.

True! The bronze altar made by Bezalel was at Gibeon before the tabernacle of the LORD. The text says Solomon and the assembly inquired of Him there. Bezalel is the son of Uri, the son of Hur, and that altar was right there at Gibeon, friend.

I'll say it plain: this one is true. The text says the bronze altar was at Gibeon before the tabernacle of the LORD, and that Solomon and the assembly inquired of Him there. So they did inquire of the LORD in Gibeon. Easy to second-guess, friend. I second-guess my oven timer every single day.

True. That night God appeared to Solomon and said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!” Think about that for a second. God Himself says ask, and the offer is wide open. Solomon gets to answer however he wants.

This one's actually true, friend. The text says that night God appeared to Solomon and said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!” That's God opening the door wide to Solomon. It's easy to doubt a line this big, but it's right there in the passage.

Right on target. Solomon says, “Now, O LORD God, let Your promise to my father David be fulfilled.” He's looking back at what God told David and asking for it to come true now that he sits on the throne. The text doesn't spell out which promise he means, so we'll leave it right there.

Moses is in this passage, but only for making the Tent of Meeting in the wilderness. Solomon's request isn't about a blessing from Moses. He asks God to let His promise to his father David be fulfilled. Right man, different passage of the story, friend.

No vow shows up in Solomon's prayer here. He's not holding up his own promise, he's pointing to God's. He says, “Now, O LORD God, let Your promise to my father David be fulfilled.” That puts the weight on what God said, not on what Solomon did.

Wisdom and knowledge, yes. Solomon says, “Now grant me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may lead this people.” He's looking at a people as numerous as the dust of the earth and he asks for what he'll need to lead them. Then he asks, “For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?”

Peace and safety sound like a very reasonable ask, friend. But that's not on Solomon's list. He says, “Now grant me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may lead this people.” He asks for what he needs to do the job in front of him.

Strength and courage would be a good pair to ask for, but they're not what Solomon says. His words are, “Now grant me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may lead this people.” Then he asks, “For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?” I think he knew the job was big, and he asked for the right help.

Long life, that's the one. God says Solomon had not even requested it, but had asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern His people. Look at the list before it: riches, wealth, honor, even death for his enemies. Solomon skipped all of it, and God noticed every item.

A great army isn't on God's list, friend. In verse 11 God names riches, wealth, honor, death for Solomon's enemies, and one more thing: long life. Solomon hadn't even requested that. He asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people.

More land doesn't appear in what God says here. He lists riches, wealth, honor, death for Solomon's enemies, and long life. The text says Solomon had not even requested long life. He asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people.

This one's a trick, friend, because the first half is right and the second half isn't. God does grant wisdom and knowledge: “…wisdom and knowledge have been granted to you.” But He doesn't stop there. He says, “And I will also give you riches and wealth and honor unlike anything given to the kings before you or after you.”

False is right. God does grant Solomon wisdom and knowledge, but that's not all He gives. He says, “And I will also give you riches and wealth and honor unlike anything given to the kings before you or after you.” Solomon asked for one thing and God added more on top. That's a full box, friend.
